article_text:
Two years after the success of Eight Seconds: Black Rodeo Culture , Damiani releases a new edition featuring 91 previously unpublished photographs, with a foreword by James Pickens Jr., Grey’s Anatomy actor and rodeo devotee.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Ivan McClellan.

Present on the ranches of the American West since the end of the Civil War, where they made up no less than a quarter of the workforce, Black cowboys have long been rendered invisible by Hollywood and the American national myth. A distortion that photographer Ivan McClellan has been dismantling for ten years, from the dusty arenas of Oklahoma to the red clay lands of Texas.

“We see the faces. The joy. The color. The pageantry. The fellowship. We witness triumph and pain, history and legacy — but above all, celebration,” writes Pickens Jr., an avid rider and organiser of team roping events across Southern California. “This is a Western lifestyle uniquely shaped by the Black cowboy and cowgirl experience.”

“It showed me how vital the Black cowboy’s story is to the true history — and mythology — of the American West,” writes Pickens Jr. in Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion , recalling his first Black rodeo in New York City forty years ago. “That experience changed my perspective. It reshaped my understanding of what it really means to be a cowboy.” It took a photographer from Portland to give the American West back its true color.

Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion by Ivan McClellan. Foreword by James Pickens Jr. Damiani Books , 112 pages, 91 color photographs. $50

Daily Newsletter

Paris Students Shut Down the Louvre

Artist Rosana Paulino makes a self-portrait of Brazil, protests in France and Colombia, and this month’s edition of Beer With a Painter.

“Brazil is a country that has never really looked at itself,” artist Rosana Paulino — one of the nation’s representatives at this year’s Venice Biennale — tells curator and researcher Daniela Mayer in an interview today. So Paulino sets herself to the task, coopting the European form of the illustrated naturalist album — “images made by foreigners for foreigners” — to represent the experience of Black Brazilian women.

All the world over, art is a flashpoint for political struggle. In Paris, art students block the entrance of the Louvre to protest France’s overcrowded and underresourced schools, Staff Repoter Anna Lee writes. In Colombia, artists are out on the streets, fighting back against the right-wing president's removal of artworks by women and LGBTQ+ artists from the national museum, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia reports. And a new film reviewed by Greta Rainbow laments Iranian authorities’ search and seizure of an archive lovingly assembled by painter and conceptual artist Nasser Bakhshi in Tabriz.

Confiscating, censoring, destroying — it’s the very antithesis of art, which safeguards memory, gives voice to the marginalized, builds something new. As Paulino puts it, “Fascism is against art, isn’t it?

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Smiles Meyer Queers “The Last Supper”

For Smiles Meyer, art is an act of divine transformation — both creatively and bodily. In 2024, the Los Angeles-based trans photographer and musician staged “The First Gathering,” in which they recreated Leonardo da Vinci’s “The Last Supper” (1495–98) with trans models. Meyer is part of a growing tradition of queer and trans artists visualizing queer identities with longstanding religious imagery, with artists like Elizabeth Ohlson Wallin recreating scenes including the Last Supper. The series builds on their previous projects like the Mary + I cover and nightclub exorcism shots taken for performance artist Maris, allowing them to unpack religious trauma through art that explores and celebrates their gender identity. | Emma Cieslik

article_text:
Archives – October 29, 2018

They names are Florence and Damien Bachelot.

They are passionate about photography and collect it.

Their collection is beautiful, engaged, humanist.

You will discover it throughout these next months in the Eye of Photography with a regular column.

Last month in South Korea, they presented at the biennial photo Daegu an exhibition organized by the curator Françoise Docquiert, here are some images, as well as the texts that accompanied the exhibition.

Jean-Jacques Naudet

Exemplary Collectors : a look at the Florence and Damien Bachelot collection

Florence and Damien Bachelot are exemplary collectors. In a little over twenty five years, they have put together one of the best collections of the twentieth century photography – today more than six hundred items- following two principles : to exclusively acquired period prints of a exceptionnal quality and to favor – with now more and more exceptions – black-and-white prints which are more abstract and serve a sort of aesthetic back-and-forth , still today a common thread through the history of photography.

At first, the Bachelot were more interested in prints made by French humanist photographers – including Brassai, Robert Doisneau, Willy Ronis, Janine Niepce and Cartier-Bresson – and then their curiosity shifted to Americans – Sid Grossman, Bruce Davidson, Nan Goldin, Saul Leiter, Joel Meyerowitz – which renforced a collection already enriched by youngers photographers such Lisa Rose, Luc Delahaye, Stephane Couturier and Ambroise Tezenas…

For them, collecting is a sort of intellectual construction, patiently built from examples, impulses, sometimes blind reactions, enthusiastic burts, more or less eccentric judgments and joyful expectations. And if the Bachelot justify their choice by successive favorites, they ultimately search for a certain coherence between the works they strive together.

The collection is thus an incentive to research and study, tied to a progression of their taste. They are always guided by intuition when going to encounter a work. The relationship with artists remains important : they try to know everything about their work, about the sincerity and consistency of their approach, about their position in the art world. Since they are alone responsible for their choices, the Bachelot develop in the direction of an assertive rigor to always express their free choice.

As private collectors, in the world of images, Florence and Damien Bachelot play a major role of counterpoint and stimulation. By showing a part of their images to a large public, they want to share a part of their rarely exhibited images.

Françoise Docquiert

The car, a symbol of modernity – Photographs from Florence and Damien Bachelot’s collection

“I think that cars today today are almost the exact equivalent of the great Gothic cathedrals; I mean the supreme creation of an era, conceived with passion by unknown artists, and consumed in image if not in usage by a whole population, which appropriates them as purely magical object.” Roland Barthes, Mythologies, 1957, translated by Annette Lavers.

The development of modern life has involved a growing space devoted to the car, viewed as much as an object of social identification as a symbol of modernity.

Who better than photography could patiently testify to these upheavals?

In the early twentieth century, the car and the camera indeed both knew, almost simultaneously, major technical developments sharing as a common point a quest for speed. The practice of automobile tourism met another one, that of amateur photography.

In such a context, it is hardly surprising that professional photographers immediately appropriated that particularly photogenic object, bearing multiple meanings. A large number of them, worldwide, took to photographing cars in their daily environment, parked on the streets of the main cities, Paris and New York among many others… These artists view the car as a kind of medium and are interested in the various aspects of its culture, such as petrol stations, car parks, garages. In these photographers’ eyes, the fascination the car exercises gets reinforced by its great visual appeal and evocative power.

The intelligence of a collection notably lies in its ability to record the mutations of its time. For Florence and Damien Bachelot, photography reveals the contemporary society and opens up a new narrative of the world. No wonder then that we can find a large number of images of cars among the six hundred pictures in their collection.

About fifty of them will be on show at Daegu 2018 biennial exhibition, depicting, through specific gazes and critical readings, fragments of a social reality illustrating more than a century of car use.

Thus Le conducteur au volant de sa voiture (The driver driving his car) by Jacques-Henri Lartigue, French painter, writer and photographer. His celebrity will wait until the 50s with a “failed” picture of a formula 1. In 1912, during the Grand Prix of the Automobile-Club of France, Lartigue is surprised by the speed of a car, he follows her viewfinder and triggers. During the development, he finds that everything is moved, deformed and that the car is badly framed. He does not shoot the photo and the fate of his archives in 1950. It’s a huge success. All that had done that the image was missed now participates in its dynamism: the blur of “shake”, the deformation of the wheels, the framing of the car that goes so fast that it is already out of the frame ….

Policier parisien réglant la circulation, place de la Madeleine (Parisian policeman regulating the traffic, Place de la Madeleine) , the nod of Robert Doisneau to the police officer of Paris, he who, from 1934 to 1939, at age 22, enters the photo service of the Renault factories in Billancourt. From these five years spent at Renault will be born a prodigious collection, precious witness of a mythical company, but also of a place and a time.

Rue de la Mare or Ménilmontant , the clichés of Willy Ronis and his cars unveil the indestructible links that have attached to the City of Light until his death in 2009, at 99 years.

Brooklyn Gang. Bruce Davidson, a huge black-and-white photographer, celebrated Brooklyn’s cars and gangs in the 1960s with formal power, a social and political dimension, and a deep humanity. Again, the car documents his shots.

More recently, Philippe Chancel, in his series Drive thru Flint , is the witness of the decay of Detroit, a long time symbol of progress with its three great giants of the automobile – General Motors, Ford and Chrysler. But from the beginning of the 80s, the car industry in the US collapsed. Detroit is renamed “Murder Capital.”

The masterful use of color photography is the hallmark of Saul Leiter, Harry Gruyaert and Joel Meyerowitz. Each of their photos reveals a clean and unique universe, built with a mastery of color, light and composition. They each took the narrative power of the car in their own way and Joel Meyerowitz confirms it: “I started to understand that the glass of the car was the frame and that, in a way, the car itself was the camera with me.”

The car will soon be able to drive without a driver. The photographic technique changes with the digital age, social networks and connected tools. Yet photographers are still fascinated by cars because this modern icon still symbolizes accelerated freedom.

Françoise Docquiert

article_text:
Kenneth Atchity, “ The Meg ” producer and literary agent, died on Monday. He was 82.

Across his career as a literary manager, producer and writer, Atchity produced more than 30 films; wrote over 20 books; negotiated publishing and entertainment deals; and published hundreds of additional titles through his own imprint, Story Merchant Books. In addition to producing “The Meg” films with his business and producing partner Chi-Li Wong, he had credits on “Gambino,” “The Kennedy Detail,” “The Lost Valentine,” “The Amityville Horror: The Evil Escapes , ” “Joe Somebody” and “Life Or Something Like It.”

Related Stories

‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories

‘I Play Rocky’ Star Anthony Ippolito on Sylvester Stallone’s Reaction, Drinking Raw Eggs and Why Hollywood Needs 'More Raw, Human Stories'

Prior to working in Hollywood, Atchity served as an assistant professor of English and comparative literature at Occidental College before earning tenure and becoming a full-time professor. During his 17 years at the college, he became a Fulbright professor of American literature at the University of Bologna; founded and edited two magazines; and was awarded Occidental’s faculty achievement award and the UCLA Writers Program’s distinguished instructor award.

Popular on Variety

Atchity also worked as a communication engineer at AT&T Long Lines, where he designed and implemented the Green Network, which connects NASA’s 26 research centers. He decided to change careers to produce “Shades of Love,” a set of 16 films which were broadcast on HBO and Cinemax and were internationally distributed by Warner Bros..

Born in Eunice, La., in 1944, Atchity was raised in Kansas City, Mo., and attended Georgetown University before entering Yale as a Woodrow Wilson Fellow, where he earned a masters in philosophy and a PhD. While there, his doctoral dissertation won the John Addison Porter prize, the university’s highest academic award, and was published with an introduction by novelist John Gardner.

Atchity is survived by his wife, Kayoko Mitsumatsu; his son, Vincent Atchity; his daughter, Rosemary Atchity; his five grandchildren, Margaret D. McKenna, Edward J. McKenna, Oliver D. Atchity, Eliot J. Atchity and Louis M. Atchity; and his sisters, Mary Calhoun and Laurie Dressman..

Donations may be made to Yoga Gives Back , an organization empowering women and children in India which Atchity served on the board for.

Nasce, cioè, per fermare il tempo. Dayanita Singh lo trasforma invece in qualcosa che non smette mai di cambiare: un organismo mobile, dentro cui le immagini intrecciano sempre nuove relazioni e raccontano ogni volta una storia diversa. Archivio , a Roma al Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, curata da Andrea Anastasio con il sostegno dell’Istituto Italiano di Cultura di New Delhi e visitabile fino al 3 gennaio 2027. Una distinzione che dice molto del suo modo di intendere l’immagine: «una fotografia è solo materia prima”, sostiene l’artista, «ha bisogno di una struttura, di un contenitore, di un’architettura. L’archivio, insomma, non si limita a custodire la memoria, in qualche modo la produce. Ed è proprio qui che archivio e fotografia finiscono per somigliarsi. Un archivio nasce per classificare, conservare, rendere reperibile ciò che altrimenti rischierebbe di andare perduto. Nasce, cioè, per fermare il tempo. Dayanita Singh lo trasforma invece in qualcosa che non smette mai di cambiare: un organismo mobile, dentro cui le immagini intrecciano sempre nuove relazioni e raccontano ogni volta una storia diversa. È da qui che prende forma Dayanita Singh. Archivio , a Roma al Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, curata da Andrea Anastasio con il sostegno dell’Istituto Italiano di Cultura di New Delhi e visitabile fino al 3 gennaio 2027. Oltre 350 fotografie ripercorrono venticinque anni del rapporto tra l’artista indiana e l’Italia e aprendo una riflessione sulla natura della fotografia, sulla memoria, sui meccanismi con cui scegliamo che cosa conservare e che cosa lasciar cadere nell’oblio.

Nata a New Delhi nel 1961, Singh arriva alla fotografia attraverso il reportage, ma se ne allontana presto. Da anni preferisce definirsi una «bookmaker working with photography», una creatrice di libri che lavora con la fotografia. Una distinzione che dice molto del suo modo di intendere l’immagine: «una fotografia è solo materia prima”, sostiene l’artista, «ha bisogno di una struttura, di un contenitore, di un’architettura. Di una forma che sia la più adatta a fruire dell’immagine». Non un oggetto da incorniciare e fissare per sempre a una parete, dunque, ma un tassello di una struttura capace di cambiare significato a seconda della sequenza e del contesto in cui viene inserita.

Già nel 2013 con File Room , Singh porta al centro del proprio lavoro gli archivi pubblici e privati dell’India: scaffali stipati di faldoni, montagne di carte, documenti avvolti nella stoffa, corridoi, stanze, e le persone che quei luoghi li abitano e li custodiscono. Non è però un censimento documentario. A interessarla sembra piuttosto il paradosso dell’archivio: costruire un ordine stabile per qualcosa – la memoria – che stabile non è mai.

Dietro ogni classificazione apparentemente neutra, del resto, c’è sempre una scelta. Qualcuno decide che cosa conservare, come catalogarlo, a che cosa attribuire importanza e che cosa lasciare ai margini. L’archivio, insomma, non si limita a custodire la memoria, in qualche modo la produce. Ed è proprio qui che archivio e fotografia finiscono per somigliarsi. Anche fotografare significa scegliere una porzione di reale, separarla dal resto e affidarla al futuro. Nel percorso di Dayanita Singh a un certo punto il libro non basta più: l’artista porta nello spazio espositivo la possibilità di montaggio e smontaggio delle immagini, costruendo strutture lignee mobili che si aprono, si chiudono, si trasformano, si ricompongono. Nasce così uno dei progetti più importanti della Singh, Museum Bhavan : i suoi “musei” sono architetture portatili, dentro cui le fotografie possono essere mostrate ma anche custodite, sostituite, riorganizzate. Il museo diventa libro, il libro diventa museo.

Da qui le sedici strutture lignee – “pillar” – esposte oggi a Villa Giulia, che custodiscono ciascuna venti immagini, la cui funzione va ben oltre quella di un semplice supporto espositivo: le fotografie possono cambiare posizione, stabilire nuovi rapporti tra loro. L’opera quindi non coincide più soltanto con l’immagine, ma comprende il dispositivo che la contiene. Tra le sedici strutture lignee ce ne sono solo due che contengono immagini a colori e una, in particolare, solo immagini di rose. Chi conosce il lavoro dell’artista indiana, sa che il colore è molto raro nelle sue immagini, i fiori lo sono ancora di più. «Non avrei mai immaginato di fotografare delle rose – racconta Dayanita Singh a exibart – in realtà ho solo scattato qualche foto a Piazza del Popolo per mia madre e ne sono rimasta conquistata. Poi sono andata al roseto dell’Aventino e sono diventata ossessionata dalle rose. All’inizio ho usato il bianco e nero, poi gradualmente è entrato il colore. Come si sa, tutti vengono in India per il colore. Beh, io ho trovato il mio colore in Italia!».

E al piano superiore di Villa Giulia c’è un altro “pillar” che contiene alcune foto a colori di reperti etruschi, fotografati appositamente, come le rose, per la mostra romana: «Lo stesso giorno in cui ho fotografato le terrecotte al Museo Etrusco, sono uscita e ho fotografato le rose. È come se fosse stato un dono da parte di Villa Giulia. Anche la locandina su cui campeggia una grande rosa rossa è un’idea concepita qui. Quindi, immagino che quando entri in uno spazio come il Museo Etrusco e ti ci soffermi – cosa che è inevitabile fare – questo si riveli e ti offra, in questo caso, una sorta di dono di colore che è una combinazione tra la luce di Roma, Villa Giulia e le rose di Piazza del Popolo».

Archivio nasce da due anni di preparazione, venticinque anni di immagini scattate da Singh in Italia e dal lavoro che, nell’ultimo decennio, l’artista ha dedicato in particolare agli archivi italiani. Architetture, interni, opere d’arte, amici, archivisti, biblioteche, depositi, luoghi privati compongono quella che il curatore Andrea Anastasio – che accompagnò Dayanita Singh nel suo primo viaggio in Italia – definisce una “cartografia relazionale” del Paese. Non un’Italia da grand tour , non un inventario sistematico, ma un territorio costruito attraverso incontri, relazioni, amicizie.

«In questi lunghi anni di frequentazione assidua dell’Italia – racconta Anastasio – Dayanita è riuscita a tessere una famiglia di amici che sono stati via via coinvolti nel suo progetto, e ha avuto così la possibilità di accedere a case, palazzi, dimensioni intime, familiari, istituzionali, in maniera straordinaria, come pochi. Gli amici le hanno affidato le loro storie, i loro interni, i loro silenzi. Sono diventati in un senso profondo i suoi mecenati». Un mecenatismo, precisa Anastasio, «non economico nel senso classico, ma di cura e di reciprocità: Singh si prende cura degli spazi e delle vite che fotografa, in cambio i suoi amici si prendono cura della sua pratica in evoluzione. Lo scambio è sottile, ma fondamentale». Ne emerge, conclude il curatore, «un archivio che abita la città con leggerezza, ascolta più di quanto dichiari. È forse questa la silenziosa radicalità dello sguardo di Dayanita Singh: in luoghi gravati dalla storia, lei trova il presente; in città sature di rappresentazione, scopre l’inaspettato».

Il progetto è stato presentato in primavera all’Archivio di Stato di Venezia e proseguirà il suo percorso in altre sedi italiane, ma ogni tappa viene ripensata in rapporto al luogo che la accoglie. Il Museo Etrusco, continua Attanasio, è stato scelto «prima di tutto per la bellezza del luogo e la possibilità di esporre in un contesto museale particolarmente connesso all’archeologia: la sedimentazione di segni e testimonianze di civiltà precedenti e la stratigrafia come documento utile alla lettura e alla comprensione che sono così importanti nel lavoro di Dayanita». Ma c’è un altro motivo che è stato decisivo nella selezione di Villa Giulia: la connessione alla letteratura per via del Premio Strega, tradizionalmente ospitato nell’emiciclo e nel mitreo del museo. «Dayanita è particolarmente legata alla letteratura e al libro come strumento di diffusione della sua pratica artistica», questa coincidenza è stata determinate per la scelta.

C’è infine una domanda molto contemporanea che attraversa il lavoro di Singh: che cosa significa archiviare oggi, quando produciamo e conserviamo una quantità di immagini infinitamente superiore a quella di qualsiasi epoca precedente? L’artista lo ha detto chiaramente: «the photographer of the future will be more of an archivist» – il fotografo del futuro sarà sempre più un archivista. Forse perché il problema non è più soltanto produrre immagini, ma capire cosa farne: quali scegliere, quali mettere in relazione, quali affidare alla memoria e quali lasciare scomparire. In un presente sommerso dalle fotografie, il gesto artistico può allora consistere nel costruire le condizioni perché le immagini possano essere fruite diversamente. L’archivio nasce per fermare il tempo, Dayanita Singh lo rimette in movimento e lo consegna al presente.

Cannes 2026 wrapped this past weekend, but the Film Comment crew has not slowed down one bit as we continue to cut through the noise with dispatches, interviews, Podcasts, a special Cannes Critics’ Grid, and much more.

For our final Podcast from the Croisette, FC Editor Devika Girish gathered three of our favorite critics—Justin Chang ( The New Yorker ), Tim Grierson ( Screen International ), and Jessica Kiang ( Variety )—to unpack the festival’s final days. article_text:
Die Kunstmesse Artissima in Turin ist immer ein guter Ort für Experimente. Die 33. Ausgabe beschwört die Kraft der Imagination

Lebe lieber ungewöhnlich, heißt es – selbst wenn das bedeutet, an einem Arm zu saugen, als wäre es ein frischer Apfel. "Sucker!" heißt dieses Bild der griechischen Malerin Amalia Vekri. Auf der 33. Artissima in Turin ist es im Programm der Una Galleria zu finden, die 2018 im italienischen Piacenza gegründet wurde – junge Kunst kann auch in der Peripherie gedeihen, so die Idee.

Typisch Artissima: Die einzige Messe in Italien, die sich ganz der zeitgenössischen Kunst widmet, ist immer ein guter Ort für Experimente – und stellt die Kunst wirklich in den Fokus. Von den 183 teilnehmenden Galerien, darunter Chert Lüdde aus Berlin, A Gentil Carioca aus Rio de Janeiro oder Continua aus San Gimignano, zeigt mehr als ein Drittel monografische Ausstellungen in ihren Kojen.

Zahlreiche Preise, gesponsert von Illy, Seletti und anderen, stützen die Qualität des Angebots. Direktor Luigi Fassi versteht seine Messe als Ort des kulturellen Austauschs und findet, dass Kunst als öffentliche Intelligenz die demokratischen Institutionen einer Gemeinschaft stärken und bereichern könne. Er beschwört die Kraft der Imagination – was sowohl für die Emerging Artists in der kuratierten Sektion "Present Future" als auch für die Werke der 1930er- bis 1990er-Jahre in der Sektion "Back to the Future" passt.

article_text:
Sacha Baron Cohen has launched an impassioned defence of satire, the right to offend, and his Ali G character on in a lengthy article for Time magazine .

On the eve of the release of his new film, Ali G: Who Iz I ?, Baron Cohen described satire as “more important than ever”, adding that “along the way, some people, instead of laughing, wince or worse, take offence.”

Comparing modern satirists to the traditional figure of the “bouffon”, Baron Cohen described satire as “the humour of the dispossessed … using biting and at times cruel humour to undermine systemic injustice”.

Having previously released films containing controversial characters including Kazakh journalist Borat Sagdiyev, Austrian fashion show presenter Brüno Gehard, and a thinly disguised Colonel Gaddafi parody called Admiral General Aladeen, Baron Cohen directly took on critics of the Ali G character, who has been criticised in the past for laughing at black street culture and described as a “black caricature” .

Baron Cohen writes: “I made this latest film for the same reason I’ve always done this work. Not only to make people laugh, but also to bring them face-to-face with the danger of fanaticism and conspiracy theories.”

He added: “I’ve always designed my characters and comedy as vehicles to expose prejudice, bias and stupidity, though I realise not everyone sees them that way. Ali G is a white imbecile – a delusional cultural appropriator – who steals the fashion and lyrics from his favourite gangsta rap and dancehall idols, from Compton to Kingston. The joke is on him, and on the predominantly white male establishment who take him seriously.”

“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him. The world he’s returned to is, in many ways, worse than the one he left 20 years ago. All the prejudices my characters are designed to expose haven’t just lingered – they’ve metastasised ... 20 years ago, Ali G would sit next to world experts spouting absurdities. Today – fed a steady diet of disinformation and conspiracy theories by social media influencers and TikTok news – we have created an entire world where ignorance reigns and truth is inverted.”

Saying that “each of my characters has a specific mechanism to encourage people to drop their guards and show what they really believe, prejudices and all”, Baron Cohen suggests that “yes, satire can offend people other than the intended targets.” Aware that the release of his new film is likely to attract protests, he said that his university dissertation was a study of Jewish and black cooperation during the 1960s struggle for civil rights in the US, and added: “As someone who has opposed bigotry and injustice throughout my life and partnered with civil rights groups, I don’t recognise myself in the warped portrayals of me that I sometimes see on social media, lumped in with the bigots I lampoon.”

Pointing to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s path from TV comic to president of Ukraine, Baron Cohen suggested that “satire doesn’t just needle politicians or regimes – it occasionally helps bring them down”, and that the Trump administration’s actions against Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel showed that “ridicule is [far from] irrelevant”.

Quoting George Orwell’s observation in his 1945 essay Funny But Not Vulgar that “every joke is a tiny revolution”, Baron Cohen concluded: “Maybe [satire] can even help shame more of our governments into finally making our Silicon Valley overlords – unelected billionaires who decide what billions of people see and believe – liable for the lies, conspiracies, and hate on their platforms that have already gotten people killed and will likely kill many more.”

“We are once again entering an age of ‘virtuous’ violence, where any atrocity – by racists, Jew-haters, or Islamophobes, the right or the left – can be somehow justified. It is not a place any of us should want to live.”

ヒラリー・クリントン、直島で草間彌生のカボチャと記念撮影。「芸術は好奇心を取り戻す解毒剤」

高松宮殿下記念世界文化賞 の授賞式典のため来日中の ヒラリー・クリントン が 直島 を訪問し、 草間彌生 のカボチャ作品との記念写真を自身のInstagramに投稿した。

元 米 大統領夫人の ヒラリー・クリントン が、第37回 高松宮殿下記念世界文化賞 の合同記者会見と授賞式典に出席するため、来日している。合同記者会見は10月27日、授賞式典は28日に東京都内で開催される。

高松宮殿下記念世界文化賞は、日本美術協会が1988年に創設した国際的な芸術賞だ。絵画、彫刻、建築、音楽、演劇・映像の5部門で、優れた業績を上げた芸術家を毎年顕彰している。各国の国際顧問による推薦をもとに、日本の選考委員会が候補者を選び、日本美術協会の理事会が受賞者を最終決定する。

クリントンは2022年、アメリカの国際顧問に就任。同国の推薦委員会委員長として、受賞候補者の推薦を担っている。前任者は元駐日大使のキャロライン・ケネディで、2018年から国際顧問を務め、駐オーストラリア大使への指名に先立ち2021年に退任した。クリントンは5人目の国際顧問にあたる。

今回の来日に際して 直島 も訪問し、10月26日にその様子をInstagramに投稿した。 草間彌生 による2点のカボチャの彫刻とともに写真に収まり、「ときに暗く混沌とする世界において、芸術は感覚の麻痺や好奇心の喪失に対する解毒剤となる。創造という営みそのものが抵抗の行為であることを思い出させてくれます」とつづった。

今年の受賞者は、絵画部門の ジェニー・ホルツァー 、彫刻部門のアンディ・ゴールズワージー、建築部門のダニエル・リベスキンド、音楽部門のヘルベルト・ブロムシュテット、演劇・映像部門のケイト・ブランシェットの5人。各受賞者には賞金1500万円と感謝状、顕彰メダルが贈られる。また、若手芸術家奨励制度の対象団体には、フランスの芸術教育団体ラ・スルス・ガルースト協会が選ばれ、奨励金500万円が贈られた。（翻訳：編集部）
